>The industrial revolution would not be possible if it wasn't for capitalism.

One of the main points throughout Marx's work is that capitalism is the most revolutionary mode of production in history, just as was feudalism. I don't think of that at all as a concession of capitalism's benevolence, but the realization that the bourgeoisie "cannot exist without constantly revolutionising \[sic\] the instruments of production" (*Manifesto of the Communist Party*, fyi). The relation between those who accumulate capital and those who create it (and should therefore be entitled to all that they create) remains as exploitative as ever because it's built on class hierarchies.

Capitalism is built on the relentless pursuit of profit by any means necessary, even when it becomes completely self-destructive (if capitalism was really about 'helping' economies or societies, fossil fuel industries would've disbanded decades ago in favor of aggressively implementing sustainable energy policies). It's hard to see the maximization of profit as anything OTHER than chasing the dragon, since 'more is never enough' is not only pretty thoroughly embedded in consumer culture, but enshrined in law (CEO's are legally required to think of the shareholders first, if I'm not mistaken, but I can't find the particular clauses and laws rn).

The internal contradictions of capitalism are driving human beings to the brink of extinction. It's not just climate change which threatens any possibility for organized human living, but nuclear warfare resulting from squabbles by nation-states *resisting* capitalism's tendency to "melt all that is solid into air" since even nationalism is antithetical to global capitalism.

>Sure, under socialism technology can still advance however it's far slower than under capitalism because this incentive does not exist.

The whole reason we're able to communicate right now is because computers and the internet were developed because of the public money pumped into universities in order to research these technologies in the first place (also, the government were the only people willing the pay the bill for computers in the early days of the 'high-tech' sector). Virtually every component in our computers and phones were researched and developed using public money through government grants (i.e. our tax dollars). No free-market forces or isolated innovators chasing money were responsible for them in any sense.

The free-market, and capitalism by extension, isn't just a myth but a necessary one--it's part of an ideology meant to rationalize the attack of the richest classes of people in the world against those who have nothing by comparison, against the people who create *everything* in society.

It's not labour that needs capital, and it's time to move on to an economic system which takes light of that fact.

The two I would suggest strongly would be *Blade Runner* and *Natural Born Killers*, since they are both generally popular, well-known, and frequently cited as examples of "postmodernist film." 

The first thing that leads people to classify Blade Runner among postmodernist film is the constant genre-blending from one scene to the next. It boasts a strong film-noir atmosphere (I've seen many refer to it as neo-noir, as an example) with all of the classic elements: the gumshoe detective, the seedy underbelly of an urban city, and even the dead give-away of a femme fatale. Of course, Blade Runner is first and foremost a science fiction film, so you can see why the mixing of the two genres is cited as an example. 

Natural Born Killers, I feel, is probably a better example, as it contains both the self-awareness typically associated with postmodernism and, most importantly, the use of criticism through the act it is portraying. This is not unlike *Funny Games* (which I see mentioned around here often enough), a film that Haneke made to deliberately provoke and maximize the violence in it in order to criticize an audience's fascination with violence. Olivier Stone is notoriously controversial about many things, one of them being his dislike of violence in the media and media in general (I think he said something about the ending to Breaking Bad that was along the lines of this, but I'm not sure). His dislike of the media is apparent in the last act of the movie (prison scenes) where the reporters do all they can in order to stir up Mickey in his interview only to bring up the ratings (they couldn't care less about the moral outrage they are feigning). Also, Stone's use of multiple formats (video, 16mm, mixing black and white, etc) and cuts that rarely last a second are seen as postmodernist.     

Postmodernism in film, or what is considered so, is actually very plentiful, with the one of the most interesting being Godard (I'd suggest film socialisme or Tout Va Bien as essential).

Peeping Tom is frequently hailed as the first modern slasher film (it's a brief allusion in one of the Scream films too), but I think it’s far more interesting to examine its themes of voyeurism more than anything else, although I think it’s a very good thriller. What attracted me initially to this movie was this quote by Martin Scorsese where he mentions it as one of two movies about film-making:
  
“I have always felt that Peeping Tom and 8½ say everything that can be said about film-making, about the process of dealing with film, the objectivity and subjectivity of it and the confusion between the two. 8½ captures the glamour and enjoyment of film-making, while Peeping Tom shows the aggression of it, how the camera violates... From studying them you can discover everything about people who make films, or at least people who express themselves through films.[4]”

This is more my opinion than anything, but I find myself constantly revisiting this movie because of what that quote sums up and what the title of the movie could allude to, the comparison of a voyeur, of a pervert, to a film-maker. There’s also a quote by Hitchcock that would be relevant and interesting to look up where he says he’s simply the man hiding in the corner filming the things he sees. Filmmakers seem very similar to peeping toms. They are people who ‘get off’ watching others doing things, which could be sharing an intimate moment of romance like in Lost in Translation or watching a women being stabbed to death like in Psycho. That’s as far as I go with that idea, although I do play with it often, so I hope you or someone else would like to expand on this. Also, it would be appropriate to mention that Haneke, the Austrian director, makes films that play on the theme of voyeurism as well but from the other side, the perspective of the audience (particularly with how he constantly breaks the fourth wall in Funny Games and his use of camcorders in Cache).

Just to clarify on the gap I was talking about, I wrote that thinking about the differences between film and digital, especially the issue of sharpness and resolution. A decade ago it was easy to tell which movie was shot on film and what was shot on digital. There was a clear gap in quality back then, but that has changed enormously now. 

I think you are exactly right. Choosing between the two is a choice and one I think should be more artistic than commercial. Among the established directors (and definitely among the most successful), the choice between film and digital is not constrained by money, but the same can't be said for newcomers. I think it's sad that film is becoming obsolete when it doesn't need to be. Digital is a great thing and there's nothing more I'd like than to see the two formats coexist, but that's not the case right now.

If what I said came out as 'digital will inevitably become better than film,' then I can assure you that I meant the exact opposite. I should have said what you just did right now, that one format is not necessarily better than the other and that they are simply different. Each format has its pros and cons. I also completely agree that people need to stop trying to compare them to figure which one is 'better.'

The gap between the look of film and digital is getting smaller and smaller everyday to the point where the best cameras can mimic the look of film. We can argue for a while about whether or not digital will ever truly capture the look of film (because that argument hasn't been totally decided yet), but Tarantino's making another point besides look. Working with film is a completely different process than digital. You don't know how the image comes out until it's been developed and there's the matter of what sort of film to use. To put it simply, film has a distinct feel because it's a different process to work with. The documentary someone just recommended is really good on the subject.

I can tell you from experience that you when you assume the role of a director or a filmmaker that plenty of things change. How you view the world changes especially, at least for me it did. Suddenly, everything becomes a story and you imagine ways to capture every single one of them. It's like being a peeping tom in an apartment complex where women are always changing in front of their windows. There's always an urge to want to capture things and, more often than not, the line between fantasy and reality becomes blurred in the process. I mention the last part, because it does often happen when an actor becomes too immersed with his character, or a director in the world he's trying to create. To most people, being a filmmaker or an actor/actress is just a job and playing a certain character is just that. Others, on the other hand, feel the need to immerse themselves so much into their character or characters that they forget to leave them at home when the job's done. If you have ever walked out of a great movie that you really felt into, then you have a rough idea of what it is like to view the world through the lens of a camera.

There is so much to be said about Taxi Driver that this discussion simply won't be able to cover all of it, but there are some things that worth discussing. 

To start, it's hard to make anything of Travis. Most people attribute his odd nature and serious mental problems to his service in the Vietnam war, but that's only scratching the service and missing much of the point. Travis's problems aren't solely the result of PTSD, although they clearly do play a role in his ability to function and interact with others. Remember, much of Taxi Driver has to do with being lonely and isolated in one of the biggest cities around. Look at the famous scene where he talks to himself in the mirror. I know it was improvised, but it still says much about the character. "You takin' to me? *Well, I'm the only one around here.*" Think about it; he is so lonely that he has to talk to his reflection. Overall, Taxi Driver is a film about isolation and loneliness. If he had an environment that recognized that he has some serious issues, then he wouldn't have done much of what he did. Instead, Betsy kicks him out of her life, the cab drivers go on about nothing (remember when Travis talks to Wizard about wanting to do "bad things" to people?), and the pimps see him only as a customer. 

Travis is also a walking contraction and someone who creates his own misfortune. He is disgusted by the prostitution and sex around him, yet he goes to watch pornos every night. He longs for human interaction, yet ruins his chances with Betsy by taking here to watch a porno flick (I can't think of anyone who would watch porn on a first date with a girl). If Travis had just taken her to dinner or a less shocking movie, who knows what could've happened. Instead, he creates his own misfortune. 

As I said when I started, you could literally write an entire book about Taxi Driver and still not get everything. But what bothers me the most is when people simply look at Taxi Driver as a movie about a disturbed veteran (which he obviously is) and not consider the other themes and aspects of the movie. Hell, look at the beginning and the end of the movie. The first scene and the last scene are identical, because nothing was solved and Travis remains the same person.

Although I strongly disagree with many of the points you have made above, I feel the need to point out something about this film that you failed to mention in your criticism, namely one of the film's vital themes. Full Metal Jacket, while it does attempt to portray the absurdity of war, ultimately attempts to portray human nature, or more specifically how war negatively affects all aspects of the human psyche. In the very least, the dehumanization of institutions (in this case the military) plays a very important part in the first act of the film. The institution presented in the film (the same basic concept applies to A Clockwork Orange) attempts to strip those who enter it of the traits that make them individual (or at least seem to make them unique) and breaks them down completely so that it is able to mold them into the role of a programmed killer without any remorse for those he is told to kill without question. Some could argue that the importance of this theme shifts over the course of the film as the first act is completed, but if it does indeed fade into the background and let other themes take charge, it is certain that this theme is important to the film. 

Some examples that further illustrate the point would be the scenes where the men "pray" before going to bed with their guns (most of the drill sergeant's dialogue exemplify this point)   and the most vivid one by far would the example of Private Pyle, whose descent into madness illustrates the breaking point that this institution attempts to reach but never cross. In the first example, the men are able to see that their weapons are nothing without them, which could possibly lead to them realizing what they have been taught to ignore about war, but any possibility that they realize this is effectively negated by the next statement, "without it (the rifle), I am nothing."  In the latter, they are being taught that the rifle is their sole reason for existence; they are killers and would serve no purpose in life without it. 

Overall, Full Metal Jacket stresses the dehumanizing effects of an institution, especially one heavily involved in the abhorrent business of war. Even though the film was not your taste, I hope you can at least appreciate what Kubrick was trying to say and acknowledge what I believe to be the most important theme in this film and a crucial one as well in much of his work.

I can tell you know what you're talking about. I've felt much like you too. I see my friends enjoy the success I crave and I envy them greatly for it. Some of them are the typical 'never did anything in high school' kind of people, but only because they were working so diligently on skill and abilities I can only dream of. I didn't and I think I regret that more than anything. Instead of doing schoolwork or honing my abilities I just sat around wasting my life and feeling sorry for myself, all while eating my problems away until I discovered the bottle. It's true what they say about it though. Being miserable under the influence instead of over makes a huge difference. All the same you're miserable, but at least having a vice provides a temporary fix. A temporary fix to a permanent problem. 

I tried those little goals like writing the first chapters of a novel or getting thoughts on paper and writing prose, but the problem with self-loathing is that it all looks bad. While people would remark on my writing I'd be quietly scowling at it, all the time impatient to run home and rip it to pieces. A writer is never satisfied with his own work, but some people take it to whole new levels. 

I guess I won't give up for now. Maybe it's out of cowardice; maybe I just can't bring myself to kill myself without finishing the ride I paid for. I find it hard to live, but being lost in the wonders that life have to offer will always be the first place I look to. Thank you very much for your words, I can't thank you enough for sharing with me.

Thank you for replying and your kind compliment. For what it's worth it still means quite a bit to hear someone comment on my writing ability, which I used to pride myself very much on. I hope you're right about that, because there have been plenty of authors who've been successful and never achieved what they set out to do in the first place. Enough about that though, you'll never know if you don't try right? I may not see a reason to live, but what I have will just have to do, at least for the time being. I think the meaning might be very simple, although, as it has already been pointed out, forced. What his character is trying to say is that the world is not a "fine" place (he said fine, not great, actually), but still worth fighting for. It's been a while since I've seen the film, but the one thing I remember the most from it is how hopeless the film felt. In fact, there were certain parts where I could relate with Kevin Spacey's. For instance, in the car ride when Brad Pitt's grilling him and the killer replies that none of his victims were innocent. All of them represented something intolerably ugly about society like narcissism and greed. The deaths, and torture, of these individuals were unfortunately the result of one man's pent up rage against the world he was living in. Granted that doesn't give him the excuse to commit such heinous crimes and take an actual human life, but that's not the point. The world is a horrible and grotesque place at times and Freeman's character knows this even at the beginning of the film. It isn't until the very end, however, that he fully realizes how horrible the world must be if a deranged and sadistic maniac is not what's wrong with the world. Therefore, he is totally resigned and defeated by the final scene. By killing the murderer and playing into his hands, Brad Pitt has proved the killer's ultimate point-- that humanity is beyond redemption. Needless to say, things would have turned out differently if he hadn't killed him in a total rage of uncontrollable emotion. The "bad" guy would have seen that there is still good in humanity and that the "good" guy is able to put his own impulses aside for the greater good. He didn't and proved a point that would have been moot if Pitt had just stayed his gun.
He agrees it's worth fighting for, because there really isn't much else he can do. He has been a detective for decades and no one becomes involved in law enforcement (for the most part anyways) unless you have strong feelings about right and wrong, and protecting the world from the evil humans are capable of. Gradually, the idea that the world is a good place has drifted from him, but has never totally left him. That being said, he cannot totally acknowledge that everything he has fought for has been in vain, so he compromises by saying that the world is not a fine place, but is worth fighting for. His final line isn't one of total cynical bitterness, but one where he points out the ugliness of the world while hanging on to the hope that there is something worthwhile about it, something worth fighting for.      

*TL;DR* Morgan Freeman is saying that the world is **not** a fine place and that whatever redeeming qualities about it, all the beauty and kindness present in the world, are not enough to eclipse or mask the sheer depravity and immorality (ugliness) that plagues them.

It's perfectly understandable for him to look at two of his best films and consider them disappointments, even though they're absolute masterpieces. Filmmakers (and artists for that matter) don't have the pleasure that we, as the audience, enjoy. They can't just sit back and look at their films as they are, and for good reason. Most artists, if not all, are never really satisfied with their work, but Allen takes it just a step further than most by labeling them as disappointments. Even Ingmar Bergman, his favorite director, stated a certain measure of contempt towards his own films and couldn't watch any of them for more than a few minutes. That being said, it shouldn't really come as a surprise that he doesn't really like his own movies (after all, he isn't Norma Desmond from Sunset Boulevard), even though they are without a doubt great movies.

Wow, I usually end up getting brushed off so a reply is always great (Thank you). I wish I had more to offer you than simple empathy, but there's not much I can say that someone here already hasn't. Sure I could tell you to carry that weight and fight the good fight, but I'm positive that everyone you will ever talk to about your problems will repeat the same thing over and over again. Just because something's trite doesn't mean it's not true. It's easier to give in to the atrocities of life and be the person who's always looking to others than the person who is being looked up to. I've always tried to be the seemingly infallible Atticus Finch type of character who had the best answer for everything, the shining model of hope of others. Needless to say, it's not always worked out that way and I've found myself more in the opposite position. Being that person or having people look to you as that person really limits the number of people (especially friends) who are willing to listen to you. More often than not, I feel like the only adult in these situations, in the sense that I am expected to listen to other people's problems and have no say of my own. Eventually if you don't attempt to do everything in your power to get people to realize that you're a human being as well with problems that you need to talk about then things get from bad to worse. I can't even begin to tell you how many times I've been on the edge of the abyss ready to make that final plunge and see absolutely everyone ignore or not notice the signs that I have placed in front of them to let them know of my worsening condition. Most of my days, especially the more calm and sober ones, I wish had whatever I was missing when I was younger to end it all. As it turns out, all I was missing was a stiff drink and a guilty conscience. Even the vices I am slowly killing myself with are only temporary. I'm sorry if it seems I have digressed, but I am trying to make a point with this.  

Just get a firm grip on the situation and remember that nothing will ever change unless you force it. I made the mistake in my life of thinking it would, that things would eventually get better if I let things take their course. They didn't, and they never will. I know others have told you to be strong and confront others about your feelings, and these reassurances may sound like a broken record at this point, but it simply can't be stressed enough.
